name: Bun and Thigh Roller

lead: The bun and thigh roller was a handheld roller device sold in the 1950s to 1970s for the hips, buttocks and thighs. Users rolled it over the skin with the aim of a smoother, slimmer-looking lower body and less visible dimpling.

The period coincided with the arrival of the word cellulite in English-language publications in the late 1960s. Mechanical massage is among the non-invasive treatments dermatology references list for cellulite, though results from massage-type approaches are reported to vary.

paras: A user holds the roller and passes it over the area in repeated strokes, typically as part of a home beauty or reducing routine alongside diet or exercise. Rolling is described as skin-surface massage that may temporarily improve circulation and surface smoothness.
Rolling is generally low risk, but firm pressure can cause temporary redness or bruising, particularly on sensitive skin or with bruising tendency.

angle.text: Users rolled the device over the hips, bun and thighs hoping to smooth dimpling and reduce the look of bulk. Any visible change is attributed to surface massage and is described as temporary.

lead: The bun and thigh roller is a handheld massage roller that was sold in the 1950s to 1970s as a home reducing device for the buttocks and thighs. It belongs to a family of mechanical massage gadgets that promised a smoother, firmer lower-body contour.

Cellulite, the dimpled appearance caused by subcutaneous fat pushing through fibrous connective tissue, is common and considered physiological, and was named by spas and beauty services from the 1920s before spreading into English-language magazines in the late 1960s, with Vogue in 1968 among the earliest references [1]. Mechanical massage and suction are listed among non-invasive cellulite therapies [1].

paras: The device is a hand-pushed roller intended for the buttocks and thighs. It was one of many mid-century home reducing gadgets sold through magazines and mail order.

Interest in anti-cellulite products grew in the West through the late 1960s, a trend some critics link to the cosmetic industry's marketing; some European magazines have been criticised for presenting cellulite as a disease while funded by companies selling anti-cellulite products [1]. Modern descendants include cellulite roller massagers sold online.
No studies found on this specific device. Mechanical massage is listed among non-invasive cellulite treatments in general references, which note that cellulite can resist many treatments [1].

timeline.event: The term cellulite is first used by spa and beauty services [1].
Vogue article marks the word's arrival in English-language print [1].
